title: The Golden State Killer Was Caught by His Cousins' DNA
central_question: Police had the Golden State Killer's DNA for decades but no name. How did his distant cousins lead them to him?
content_notes: Closed case: DeAngelo pleaded guilty on 29 Jun 2020 and was sentenced on 21 Aug 2020. The crimes are referred to only in summary ('dozens of crimes, including 13 murders'); they are never described or depicted, and no victim, survivor or family member is named, shown or implied. DeAngelo appears only as an anonymous rim-lit silhouette with no face or likeness. Investigators and genealogists are generic figures and are not named. Streets, the store car park, the house and the hearing room are generic illustrations, not the real places; no store brand, police badge, court document, warrant or website logo is imitated. The hero object (a crime-scene DNA vial) is a generic illustrated tube with our own typed label. No dialogue is invented. Legal status verified 2026-10-11.

lines.text: For decades, police had his DNA, but no name.
So they went looking for his cousins.
They called him the Golden State Killer.
He committed dozens of crimes from 1975 to 1986, including 13 murders.
Investigators uploaded his DNA to a free genealogy site: GEDmatch.
It didn't find the killer.
It found distant cousins.
So they built family trees,
and narrowed them by age and location.
The trees led to one man.
Joseph James DeAngelo.
The twist? He was once a police officer.
He was fired in 1979, accused of shoplifting a hammer and dog repellent.
Now they needed his own DNA.
They followed him to a store, and swabbed his car's door handle.
Then they took a tissue from his trash.
The DNA was a conclusive match.
On April 24th, 2018, police arrested him outside his home.
In 2020, he pleaded guilty to 13 murders,
at a hearing held in a university ballroom.
His sentence: life without parole, eleven times over.
Decades of hiding,
ended by a family tree and a tissue in the trash.
Next: the Great Train Robbery, and a Monopoly board.

claims.text: Investigators searched a public genealogy database for the killer's relatives. DeAngelo had never submitted his own DNA to a genealogy database; the lead came from DNA profiles that distant relatives had uploaded and shared on GEDmatch.

The crimes he admitted were committed in California between 1975 and 1986: dozens of crimes, including 13 murders (he pleaded guilty to 13 counts of first-degree murder and admitted dozens of uncharged crimes). Summary only; no detail used.

For decades the killer's crime-scene DNA sat in evidence (collected in the 1970s-80s; DNA profiles later linked the crimes), but it matched no one in the FBI's national DNA database or California's databank, so investigators had no name. He had never been arrested for an offence that put his DNA on file.

Investigators used crime-scene DNA to create a profile (reportedly under a pseudonym) on GEDmatch, a free public genealogy website where people upload and share DNA profiles to find relatives. GEDmatch said this was done without its knowledge.
GEDmatch returned distant relatives of the killer, reported as roughly third- to fourth-cousin matches.
From those matches, investigators built family trees (reported as more than 25) and narrowed them to men of the right age who had lived in the right areas, which led to DeAngelo.
The suspect identified was Joseph James DeAngelo, then 72, of Citrus Heights, a suburb of Sacramento.
FUN FACT: DeAngelo had been a police officer in two small California towns, Exeter and Auburn, between 1973 and 1979, so he was still an officer when the crimes began (1975).
He was fired from the Auburn police in 1979 after being accused of shoplifting a hammer and a can of dog repellent from a store.

On 18 April 2018, according to the unsealed affidavit, detectives followed DeAngelo to a store in Roseville and swabbed the driver's-side door handle of his car while he shopped; the sample pointed to a match.
On 23 April 2018, investigators took a tissue from the trash outside his home; per the warrant, its DNA provided the conclusive match to the crime-scene profile.
DeAngelo was arrested outside his home in Citrus Heights (reported as in his driveway) on 24 April 2018. He was 72.

On 29 June 2020 he pleaded guilty to 13 counts of first-degree murder and 13 counts of kidnapping to commit robbery, and admitted 161 uncharged crimes, which could no longer be charged because of the statute of limitations. The deal took the death penalty off the table.
FUN FACT: the plea hearing was held in a ballroom at Sacramento State university, used as a makeshift courtroom to allow social distancing during COVID-19.

On 21 August 2020, Judge Michael Bowman sentenced him to 11 consecutive life terms without the possibility of parole, plus further terms (reported by AP as 15 life terms with the possibility of parole and eight years).

Next-case tease: in the Great Train Robbery (8 August 1963) a gang stole about 2.6 million pounds from a Royal Mail train; fingerprints on a Monopoly board at their farm hideout helped lead police to them. (Narration names only the robbery and 'a Monopoly board'; the card shows the amount.)
